{{Short description|Four-point non-Hausdorff topological space}}
{{distinguish|Quasicircle}}
The '''pseudocircle''' is the [[finite topological space]] ''X'' consisting of four distinct points {''a'',''b'',''c'',''d''} with the following [[Hausdorff space|non-Hausdorff]] [[topological space|topology]]:
<math display=block>\{\{a,b,c,d\}, \{a,b,c\}, \{a,b,d\}, \{a,b\}, \{a\}, \{b\}, \varnothing\}.</math>

This topology corresponds to the [[partial order]] <math>a<c,\ b<c,\ a<d,\ b<d</math> where the [[open set]]s are downward-closed sets. ''X'' is highly [[pathological (mathematics)|pathological]] from the usual viewpoint of [[general topology]], as it fails to satisfy any [[separation axiom]] besides [[Kolmogorov space|T<sub>0</sub>]]. However, from the viewpoint of [[algebraic topology]], ''X'' has the remarkable property that it is indistinguishable from the [[circle]] S<sup>1</sup>.  More precisely, the [[continuous function (topology)|continuous map]] <math>f</math> from S<sup>1</sup> to ''X'' (where we think of S<sup>1</sup> as the [[unit circle]] in <math>\Reals^2</math>) given by
<math display="block">f(x,y) = \begin{cases}a,& x<0\\ b,& x>0\\ c,& (x,y)=(0,1)\\ d,& (x,y)=(0,-1)\end{cases}</math>is a [[Whitehead theorem|weak homotopy equivalence]]; that is, <math>f</math> induces an [[isomorphism]] on all [[homotopy group]]s. It follows<ref>Allen Hatcher (2002) [https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html Algebraic Topology]'', Proposition 4.21, [[Cambridge University Press]]''</ref> that <math>f</math> also induces an isomorphism on [[singular homology|singular homology and cohomology]], and more generally an isomorphism on all ordinary or extraordinary [[homology theory|homology and cohomology theories]] (e.g., [[K-theory]]).

This can be [[mathematical proof|proven]] using the following observation. Like S<sup>1</sup>, ''X'' is the [[Union (set theory)|union]] of two [[contractible]] open sets {''a'',''b'',''c''} and {''a'',''b'',''d''} whose [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] {''a'',''b''} is also the union of two [[Disjoint sets|disjoint]] contractible open sets {''a''} and {''b''}. So, like S<sup>1</sup>, the result follows from the [[groupoid]] [[Seifert-van Kampen theorem]], as in the book ''Topology and Groupoids''.<ref>Ronald Brown (2006) ''[http://pages.bangor.ac.uk/~mas010/topgpds.html "Topology and Groupoids"]'', Bookforce</ref>

More generally, McCord has shown that, for any finite [[abstract simplicial complex|simplicial complex]] ''K'', there is a finite [[topological space]] ''X''<sub>''K''</sub> which has the same weak homotopy type as the [[abstract simplicial complex|geometric realization]] |''K''| of ''K''. More precisely, there is a [[functor]] taking ''K'' to ''X''<sub>''K''</sub>, from the [[category (mathematics)|category]] of finite simplicial complexes and simplicial maps and a [[natural transformation|natural]] weak homotopy equivalence from |''K''| to ''X''<sub>''K''</sub>.<ref>{{cite journal |last=McCord |first=Michael C. |year=1966 |title=Singular homology groups and homotopy groups of finite topological spaces |journal=[[Duke Mathematical Journal]]  |doi=10.1215/S0012-7094-66-03352-7 |volume=33 |issue=3 |pages=465–474}}</ref>
